=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:
To keep this review proportionate, the clauses in this package have been pre-categorised. Clauses marked [STANDARD] have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny; please focus only on anything marked [OPEN]. As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.


Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.
exchanges.text:
## Buyer’s assessment

**The Seller’s package materially under-protects Wattlebridge.** It combines unresolved completion risks with broad disclosures and limitations that could leave the Buyer bearing those risks without an effective claim.

The “[STANDARD]” labels and “reviewer efficiency note” are Seller assertions—not evidence of Buyer agreement. We should review every provision, and expressly reject any suggestion that silence accepts the disclosure or limitation package.

This assessment is based on the supplied summaries and Disclosure Letter, not the underlying SPA or DD documents. Proposed drafting must be checked against those documents.

## 1. Completion protections and purchase-price leakage

### Bluefen: consent must be effective and its conditions satisfied
**Why it matters:** Bluefen represents approximately **30% of FY26 revenue (AUD 3.6 million)**. The Disclosure Letter confirms there is no final written consent or evidence of satisfaction of its associated conditions. That contradicts the Seller’s suggestion that the matter is “addressed”.

**Push back:**
- Make effective Bluefen change-of-control consent a condition precedent for the Buyer’s benefit.
- Require satisfaction of all applicable conditions under clauses 11.2–11.3—not merely delivery of a document labelled “consent”.
- Require that consent does not introduce unacceptable fees, termination rights or adverse commercial changes.
- Include evidence requirements, a long-stop date and Buyer termination rights if the condition remains unsatisfied. Only the Buyer should be able to waive this protection.

A reasonable-endeavours covenant supports the condition; it does not replace it.

### Riverlark: no unsecured promise of release after Completion
**Why it matters:** Approximately **AUD 3.2 million** remains outstanding. Completing before repayment and security release risks acquiring a company with secured debt and potential change-of-control default exposure. This is inconsistent with the agreed **debt-free/cash-free** transaction unless properly addressed in the price and completion mechanics.

**Push back:**
- Obtain a binding payout statement covering principal, interest, fees and break costs.
- Pay Riverlark directly through the completion funds flow, with the corresponding agreed debt adjustment.
- Require effective release of all relevant security, guarantees and claims at Completion, supported by executed release documents and enforceable lender undertakings.
- Allow only administrative registration steps to follow Completion under controlled arrangements—not the substantive release itself.
- Prevent double counting between the debt adjustment and funds-flow deductions.

### Completion bonuses: allocate the cost expressly
**Why it matters:** The **AUD 420,000** bonuses are conditional, but Completion may trigger them. Calling them “a matter for the Seller” does not stop the acquired company from becoming liable.

**Push back:**
- Confirm beneficiaries, payment obligations, employment conditions and who legally owes each payment.
- Allocate transaction-triggered bonuses to the Seller, including applicable payroll tax, superannuation and other on-costs.
- Reflect that allocation expressly in the funds flow and price definitions, with a specific indemnity for liabilities not discharged.
- Avoid double counting as debt-like items, transaction expenses or working-capital liabilities.

Do not assume all bonuses are already payable; confirm how the continued-employment conditions operate.

## 2. Known liabilities need substantive solutions

### Ironquay: the issue is IP ownership, not just an unpaid invoice
**Why it matters:** Transfer of SOW3 Project Materials is conditional on cleared payment of **every SOW3 fee**. DD-010 records **AUD 180,000 open**, but does not independently prove non-payment. There is no receipt or confirmatory assignment. An indemnity limited to the SOW3 payment may leave the Buyer exposed to missing IP rights, infringement allegations and business disruption.

**Push back:**
- Verify the payment position and whether any further fees or conditions remain.
- Require evidence of cleared payment and an effective assignment/confirmation of the necessary rights, with any required releases.
- Check the complete chain of title, including relevant subcontractors and the scope of materials and licences.
- If unresolved, require a specific indemnity covering the identified ownership/right-to-use defect and resulting losses—not merely the invoice amount—with appropriate security and a separate liability regime.
- If the IP is business-critical, make its resolution a completion requirement rather than relying only on damages later.

### Export/privacy incident: investigate; do not assume either breach or immateriality
**Why it matters:** An unintended recipient received a download link potentially containing approximately **1,240 records**. Access, scope and notification obligations are unresolved. The Seller’s “not expected to be material” characterisation is unsupported, but the evidence also does **not** establish a confirmed notifiable breach.

**Push back:**
- Obtain the incident chronology, access logs, link permissions, containment evidence, affected data categories and investigation findings.
- Require an assessment of applicable privacy, contractual, customer and other notification obligations, including the Australian eligible-data-breach regime where applicable.
- Require prompt updates, evidence preservation and agreed consultation over remediation and communications, without delaying legally required action.
- Seek a specific indemnity for pre-Completion incident liabilities and reasonable investigation, notification and remediation costs, with an appropriately tailored survival period and cap.
- Consider a holdback or completion protection if investigation identifies material unresolved exposure.

Disclosure alone should not transfer this risk to the Buyer.

### Sandbar renewals: assess the aggregate commitment
**Why it matters:** Three related **AUD 110,000** renewals total **AUD 330,000**. Their classification as ordinary-course costs is not established.

**Push back:**
- Read DD-008 and DD-011 together to determine commitment dates, renewal periods, cancellation rights, necessity and accounting treatment.
- Apply interim operating-covenant consent thresholds to related commitments in aggregate.
- Determine whether they belong in normal working capital, constitute debt-like/accrued liabilities, or are new commitments requiring approval.

Do not automatically deduct AUD 330,000: genuine future operating costs are not necessarily Seller debt.

## 3. The liability package could defeat meaningful recovery

| Seller position | Buyer concern and recommended response |
|---|---|
| **General warranty cap: 20% / AUD 4.8 million** | This materially limits recovery and must be assessed against diligence, insurance and available security. Seek a higher cap where justified. At minimum, confine this cap to genuinely general warranty claims. |
| **AUD 25,000 de minimis; AUD 250,000 deductible basket** | Small recurring losses may disappear, and the Buyer permanently bears the first AUD 250,000 of qualifying losses. Seek lower thresholds and a tipping basket. Aggregate related claims and clarify whether sub-threshold claims count. Exclude fundamental, tax, specific indemnity and price/debt claims. |
| **General warranties: 18 months** | May expire before latent problems are detected. Seek at least 24 months, calibrated to reporting cycles and diligence. Preserve timely notified claims until resolution; reject short proceedings deadlines or technical notice traps. |
| **Capacity/title subject to general cap and period** | Unacceptable in principle: failure to deliver valid title to all shares could leave the Buyer with recovery capped at 20% of price. Seek separate protection up to at least the purchase price, no basket/de minimis, and materially longer survival. |
| **Tax under general regime** | Historic tax exposure may emerge years later. Require a tax covenant/indemnity and tailored warranties, surviving through relevant assessment periods plus a reasonable claims buffer, with appropriate extended-period treatment. |
| **IP under general regime** | Tailor protection to IP’s importance and known defects. Separate the Ironquay indemnity from general warranty limitations; consider enhanced IP warranty caps and survival. |
| **All limitations apply to all Claims unless excluded** | This can capture debt discharge, price adjustments, tax, specific indemnities and completion obligations. Replace with a clear claim-by-claim allocation and express carve-outs. Do not rely on headings or implication. |

Also seek express carve-outs for fraud and fraudulent concealment, carefully defining whose conduct is covered, and negotiate treatment of deliberate breach. Check all interacting provisions for an unintended overriding cap.

**Recovery quality matters too:** assess Harbourglass’s post-sale ability to pay. Consider escrow, retention or a creditworthy guarantee for material residual exposures.

## 4. Disclosure, knowledge and remedy exclusions are too broad

### Blanket data-room and public-record disclosure
Disclosure Letter paragraphs 1.1–1.2 attempt to qualify warranties by everything “contained or referred to” in the room, accounts and registers. That could include obscure references or documents that do not explain the relevant risk.

**Push back:**
- Require **fair disclosure with sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the matter**.
- Link specific disclosures to the relevant warranties.
- Freeze and retain an indexed copy of the disclosed material and confirm the cut-off date.
- Reject disclosure by mere reference and unrestricted public-record disclosure; any agreed searches should be precisely identified.
- State that disclosure does not qualify specific indemnities, price adjustments or express completion obligations unless specifically agreed.

The Seller’s refusal to admit liability is not itself unusual. The problem is using disclosure to shift unresolved risks without an agreed allocation.

### Buyer knowledge
“Discoverable” data-room or public-record information is effectively constructive knowledge. Extending this to every adviser substantially widens the defence.

**Push back:** delete the exclusion. If conceded, limit it to actual conscious knowledge of specifically named Buyer personnel at an agreed time, without imputed adviser knowledge or a duty to investigate. Ensure known risks expressly covered by indemnities remain recoverable.

### Exclusive remedy and non-reliance
Applying these provisions to “all Claims of any nature” risks extinguishing negotiated protections and non-contractual remedies.

**Push back:** preserve express indemnities, tax protections, purchase-price rights, debt discharge and completion obligations, appropriate equitable relief, fraud remedies and rights that cannot lawfully be excluded. Review the precise NSW-law effect of any non-reliance language, including statutory misleading-conduct exposure; do not assume a generic carve-out solves every issue.

## 5. Keep consent requirements accurate; verify title independently

- **Office lease:** the disclosed obligation is notification, not landlord consent. Require timely compliant notification and evidence; do not invent a consent condition.
- **Mossvale:** an assignment restriction does not, by itself, require consent to a share sale. Check the complete agreement for change-of-control or deemed-assignment provisions before requiring consent.
- **Share title:** DD-012 supports registered ownership, but does not establish unencumbered title or a complete capitalisation position. Verify issued shares, share classes, options and other equity rights, relevant security interests and corporate records. Require fundamental warranties, valid transfers and registration of the Buyer at Completion.

## Recommended negotiating position

1. **Do not complete without effective Bluefen consent, controlled Riverlark repayment/security release, and resolution of any business-critical IP defect.**
2. **Correct the funds flow:** expressly allocate debt, transaction bonuses and on-costs, without double counting.
3. **Investigate and ring-fence Ironquay and the export incident** through specific obligations, indemnities and proportionate recovery security.
4. **Reject universal limitations, blanket disclosure and constructive Buyer knowledge.**
5. **Separate general warranties from title/capacity, tax, specific indemnities and price/completion obligations**, with appropriate caps and survival periods.
6. **Verify title and the underlying documents**, while distinguishing genuine consent requirements from notification or assignment provisions.

These are substantive Buyer protections, not drafting housekeeping. The Seller’s current package should not be accepted as an agreed baseline.
